content: A chemical substance is a material with a specific and definite chemical composition. This concept was solidified in the late 18th century, largely due to the work of chemist Joseph Proust. Proust demonstrated that all samples of a given compound have the same composition, meaning they contain the same proportions of elements by mass. This principle is now known as the law of constant composition. Over time, advancements in chemical synthesis, particularly in organic chemistry, as well as the discovery of new elements and the development of analytical techniques for isolating and purifying substances, contributed to the establishment of modern chemistry. Despite this, there are some debates about the definition of a chemical substance, as the vast number of substances reported in the literature requires systematic indexing. A common example of a chemical substance is pure water, which always has the same properties and the same ratio of hydrogen to oxygen, regardless of whether it is obtained from a natural source or synthesized in a laboratory. A pure chemical substance cannot be separated into other substances without a chemical reaction and is rarely found in nature in its pure form. Examples of typical chemical substances include diamond, gold, sodium chloride (table salt), and sucrose (sugar). Chemical substances, often referred to as pure substances, are defined in most general chemistry textbooks as materials with a definite chemical composition. According to this definition, a chemical substance can be a pure element or a pure compound. However, there are exceptions. For instance, alloys with uncertain compositions and nonstoichiometric compounds challenge the strict definition of a pure substance. Nonstoichiometric compounds, such as palladium hydride, do not adhere to the law of constant composition, making it difficult to distinguish them from mixtures in some cases. An element is a chemical substance composed of only one type of atom. It cannot be broken down or transformed into another element through chemical reactions, although nuclear reactions can transmute one element into another. All atoms of an element have the same number of protons, though they may differ in the number of neutrons, resulting in isotopes. There are approximately 120 known elements, about 80 of which are stable and do not undergo radioactive decay. Some elements can exist in multiple forms, known as allotropes, such as oxygen (O₂) and ozone (O₃). Most elements are metals, characterized by their luster, electrical and thermal conductivity, malleability, and ductility. Examples include iron, copper, and gold. Non-metals, such as carbon, nitrogen, and oxygen, lack these metallic properties and tend to form negative ions (anions). Metalloids, such as silicon, exhibit properties intermediate between metals and non-metals. A chemical compound is a pure chemical substance composed of two or more elements chemically bonded together. These compounds can consist of molecules or crystalline structures where atoms, molecules, or ions form a lattice. Compounds containing carbon and hydrogen are classified as organic compounds, while all others are inorganic. Organometallic compounds contain bonds between carbon and metals. Covalent compounds involve shared electrons, while ionic compounds, or salts, consist of oppositely charged ions. In organic chemistry, compounds with the same molecular formula but different structures are called isomers. Isomers, such as glucose and fructose, have distinct chemical properties and do not spontaneously convert into one another. However, tautomers, such as the open-chain and ring forms of glucose, can interconvert spontaneously, making it impossible to isolate a pure form of one tautomer. All matter is composed of elements and chemical compounds, but these are often mixed together to form mixtures. Mixtures do not have a fixed composition and can be separated into their components through mechanical processes. For example, butter, soil, and wood are mixtures. A mixture of iron and sulfur can be separated using a magnet, as no chemical reaction occurs between the two. However, if iron and sulfur are heated together in a specific ratio, a chemical reaction produces iron(II) sulfide (FeS), a compound with distinct properties that cannot be separated by mechanical means. The term chemical substance is a technical term used primarily by chemists, while the word chemical is more broadly used in industries, government, and society. The term chemical often refers to artificial or processed substances, including mixtures, and is commonly associated with products of the chemical industry. Every chemical substance has one or more systematic names, typically following the International Union of Pure and Applied Chemistry (IUPAC) naming rules. The Chemical Abstracts Service (CAS) also provides an alternative naming system. Many substances are also known by simpler, common names, such as glucose or Naproxen. Chemists often use chemical formulas or molecular structures to refer to compounds. The number of known chemical compounds has grown significantly, with approximately 30 million compounds reported in the scientific literature. To manage this vast number, organizations like IUPAC and CAS have developed systems for naming and indexing substances. CAS assigns a unique numerical identifier, known as a CAS registry number, to each reported substance. Other systems, such as SMILES and InChI, have also been developed for computer-friendly representation of chemical information. In many cases, a pure substance must be isolated from a mixture, either from natural sources or as a product of a chemical reaction.
